correctness.rationale: For a fixed priority order, deleting any vertex lowers the greedy matching count by zero or one: prove by induction on first edge, whether incident or not. This implies expectation loss at most two for deleting the two candidate endpoints, and at most one if an endpoint is isolated. Conditioning on the first accepted edge yields the exact recursion (m+1)Delta=1+mu(G-u-v)-mu(G)+sum_{f disjoint from u,v}Delta(G-V(f),e). Induct on m: all summands at most one; for k incident old edges at most one, all terms nonnegative; for k at least two, numerator at least -1-q/3, implying Delta>=-1/3. Sharp P4 and edgeless examples. The standalone checker independently passed 945204 exact rational/permutation assertions on all graphs up to six vertices (orders verified for small graphs). Finite checks are not the universal proof.

originality.rationale: A universal sharp one-edge perturbation bound for random-edge greedy matching is a different quantified statement from random-graph algorithm comparisons and approximation-ratio bounds. Inaccessible full text of a closely relevant 1997 work leaves a specific priority risk; novelty is qualified, not claimed exhaustively.

value.rationale: Sharp graph-uniform perturbation bounds measure the stability of a classical randomized greedy matching algorithm. The result explains a genuine performance paradox under adding an allowed edge, finds its optimal damage constant, and isolates a structurally nonharmful class of insertions. All finite simple graphs are classified by the theorem, not just a narrow numerical experiment. No generalization beyond this natural operation is asserted.
